title: Concurrent Use of Low‐Dose Aspirin and Omega‐3 Fatty Acids and Risk of Upper Gastrointestinal Complications: A Cohort Study with Nested Case–Control Analysis

sections.abstract: <jats:title>Abstract</jats:title><jats:p>The risk of upper gastrointestinal complications (<jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">UGIC</jats:styled-content>) due to low‐dose aspirin (<jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">LDA</jats:styled-content>) can be further increased by the concurrent exposure to other antithrombotic agents. Little is known on the combined therapy with <jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">LDA</jats:styled-content> and medications containing omega‐3 (<jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">OM</jats:styled-content>3) fatty acids, which also exert antiplatelet activity. The aim of this study was to investigate the risk of <jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">UGIC</jats:styled-content> in patients exposed to <jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">LDA</jats:styled-content>–<jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">OM</jats:styled-content>3 combination. The Italian Health Search IMS Health Longitudinal Patients Database was used to perform a population‐based cohort study. Patients aged ≥18 years with cardio‐ or cerebrovascular ischaemic disease recorded between 2002 and 2012 (cohort entry) were selected. All <jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">UGIC</jats:styled-content> cases (index date) observed up to December 2013 were identified. According to a nested case–control analysis, up to 10 controls were matched to each case on age, sex and calendar period. The risk of <jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">UGIC</jats:styled-content> was investigated among current (up to 30 days preceding index date), recent (31–60 days) and past users (61–365 days) of the <jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">LDA</jats:styled-content>–<jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">OM</jats:styled-content>3 combination. Exposure assessment was lagged by 30 days to minimize reverse causation. Additionally, a duration–response analysis was performed. Odds ratios (<jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">OR</jats:styled-content>) and 95% confidence intervals (<jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">CI</jats:styled-content>) were estimated using conditional logistic regression. Non‐users of the <jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">LDA</jats:styled-content>–<jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">OM</jats:styled-content>3 combination were the reference category. Current (<jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">OR</jats:styled-content> = 0.66; 95% <jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">CI</jats:styled-content>: 0.44–1.00), recent (<jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">OR</jats:styled-content> = 0.83; 95% <jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">CI</jats:styled-content>: 0.52–1.33) and past users (<jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">OR</jats:styled-content> = 0.81; 95% <jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">CI</jats:styled-content>: 0.57–1.15) did not statistically significantly increase the risk of <jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">UGIC</jats:styled-content>. No duration–response relationship was found. Our results suggest that <jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">LDA</jats:styled-content>–<jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">OM</jats:styled-content>3 combination therapy does not affect the <jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">UGIC</jats:styled-content> risk in patients with cardio‐ or cerebrovascular ischaemic diseases. Given the novelty of these findings, further studies are needed.</jats:p>
